title: Euphoria
synopsis: You're 20 in East Highland, two years into recovery, working a coffee shop with a sponsor on speed dial. Tonight's meeting is the first you've gone to alone. The town has not gotten quieter.

nodes.text: Basement of St. Bart's. Fluorescent hum, folding chairs, coffee that tastes like the urn it came out of. You get there twenty minutes early because early is the only way you know how to arrive anywhere alone. Headphones in, nothing playing. Somebody's laughing about a parking ticket. Then the door, and a blond ponytail, and it's Cassie Howard holding a cup with both hands.

choices.text: Stay; recovery is bigger than your discomfort
choices.consequence: You leave your coat on the chair and your feet on the floor. Two years ago you'd have been in the parking lot before the door finished closing.

choices.text: Step outside for one minute
choices.consequence: You go out into cold air that smells like somebody's cigarette and stand there working out whether stepping outside counts as leaving.

nodes.text: She sits two seats down, then moves one closer during the readings. Her mascara has been repaired at some point today and not well. When the hour breaks she's in front of you holding coffee she isn't drinking, and she says, can we talk after. You have not spoken to her since a bathroom at a party junior year, in a version of your life you don't visit.

choices.text: Agree to talk
choices.consequence: You say yes before you've decided to, and the relief that goes across her face is so complete it embarrasses you both.

choices.text: Say 'maybe' and see how the hour goes
choices.consequence: You give her a maybe, which is honest, and you watch her receive it as a no, and you let her keep it.

nodes.text: Ali picks up on the second ring, which he does, on a Tuesday, at eight at night, always. You tell him there's a person here from before. He's quiet long enough that you check the screen. Then: you called me from the sidewalk instead of driving somewhere, so let's be clear about what's actually happening here. A pause. Go back in. Sit by the door if you have to.

choices.text: Go back inside steadily
choices.consequence: You go back down the stairs and take the seat nearest the door exactly as instructed, and the exit stays an exit, and you don't use it.

choices.text: Stay outside for the meeting
choices.consequence: You stay on the step and listen to the murmur coming through the window, which is not nothing, and is also not the room.

nodes.text: You say your name and that this is the first one you've come to by yourself. That's the whole share, maybe twenty seconds. Nobody claps, which is correct. Afterward a woman named Marsha with reading glasses on a chain says glad you're here with no weight on it at all, the way you'd tell a stranger their shoelace is untied. You have to look at the floor.

choices.text: Stay for fellowship after
choices.consequence: You help stack chairs and end up in a long conversation about somebody's terrible dog, and half an hour goes by without you narrating yourself to yourself.

choices.text: Slip out quickly
choices.consequence: You're in the car before the last chair is up, and then you sit in the lot with the engine off for a while, which is its own kind of staying.

nodes.text: Back row, hood up, notebook. Lexi. You'd know that posture from across a parking lot. She's not here for herself, she's here the way people are here for somebody else, which means she drove. She catches your eye and gives you one inch of a nod, no smile. Both Howard sisters in a church basement on a Tuesday night. You'd have laughed at that once.

choices.text: Talk to Lexi first
choices.consequence: You go to the back row because it's the easier of the two conversations, and Lexi lets you have the easy thing without once pointing out that it's the easy thing.

choices.text: Talk to both sisters at once
choices.consequence: You take both of them at the same time so neither gets a private version of you, and it's unbearable for four minutes and then it isn't.

nodes.text: Ten at night, diner counter, four stools: you, Lexi, Cassie, Marsha. Pancakes nobody's eating except Marsha, who eats with the calm of a woman who has done a thousand of these nights. Cassie cries into hers without any sound. Nobody comments. Lexi reaches over, puts a hand around her sister's wrist, and leaves it there while she keeps talking about something else entirely.

choices.text: Tell Cassie you're glad she's sober
choices.consequence: You say it plainly with no history attached to it, and Cassie nods down at her plate and can't answer, and that not answering is the answer.

choices.text: Tell Lexi you're glad she's here too
choices.consequence: You say it and Lexi says where else, like it's obvious, and you understand she has been doing this quietly for months without telling anyone.

nodes.text: Wednesday, six a.m., the espresso machine doing its long complaint while it heats. Fez runs the schedule now, which nobody predicted, least of all Fez. He puts you on mornings on purpose and never says why, so your afternoons stay open for meetings and your nights end early. He pins the schedule up without comment. He has never once asked how you're doing in a way that requires an answer.

choices.text: Tell Fez about the meeting
choices.consequence: You tell him you went alone and he says good and hands you the milk pitcher and doesn't turn it into a thing, which is precisely why you told him.

choices.text: Stay quiet at work and write later
choices.consequence: You keep it in your pocket the whole shift and put it on paper at midnight, where it fits the shape it actually is better than it would have out loud.

nodes.text: The notebook is a ninety-nine-cent one from the pharmacy, because the nice ones make you feel like you owe them something. You write: I went to a meeting alone and I came home alone and I did not use. It's a boring sentence. You read it three times and it stays true every time. That part is new. Not the not-using. The believing the sentence.

choices.text: Buy a second notebook for the year
choices.consequence: You buy a second one before the first is half full, which is the most optimistic thing you have done with money in about six years.

choices.text: Start texting one line a day to Ali
choices.consequence: You start sending Ali one sentence a night. He answers some and not others, and the ones he skips still get read, and you know that.

nodes.text: Jules is at her dad's for the week. The first call is four minutes of both of you being polite, which is worse than fighting. The second is at one in the morning and she says the thing about junior year and you say your part of it out loud for the first time. On the third call neither of you mentions the past at all. You just talk. Ninety minutes.

choices.text: See her
choices.consequence: You meet at the diner on Fourth and it's easy for an hour and hard for ten minutes, and neither of you leaves early to make it stop.

choices.text: Wait to see her until you've talked to Ali
choices.consequence: You call Ali first, which delays it four days, and he asks you one question you can't answer, and you go anyway with the question still in your pocket.

nodes.text: Your mom comes into the kitchen at seven and stops in the doorway because you're already up, making her coffee, two sugars, the way she takes it. She sits down. She doesn't say anything about you being up. She hasn't said anything about it in a long time now, and this morning you finally understand that the not-saying is a discipline, and that she started it before you did.

choices.text: Tell her you love her plainly
choices.consequence: You say it in a flat morning kitchen with no occasion attached, and she sets the mug down and has to look out the window for a second.

choices.text: Cook her breakfast in return
choices.consequence: You make eggs badly and she eats every bite and says they're good, and neither of you brings up a single one of the years.

nodes.text: Gia's a sophomore, taller than you now, quiet in a way she wasn't at thirteen. When you come in after nine she looks at your face first and then, fast, at your hands, before she says hi. She's checking. She's been checking since the year she found the door open at three in the morning. She isn't sure yet. Her not being sure is not a shortage of love. It's the shape love takes afterward.

choices.text: Take Gia somewhere fun on Saturday
choices.consequence: You take her to the arcade two towns over and she is embarrassed for twenty minutes and then she is fourteen again for two whole hours.

choices.text: Apologize directly for the years
choices.consequence: You name specific nights instead of apologizing in general, which is much harder, and she says I know, and then later, from her room, thank you.

nodes.text: Two years. Marsha calls it and there's the plastic sound of a chip going around a table. You almost don't take it. The last one you held you threw into a drainage ditch on the drive home, and what came after was the worst nine months of your family's life. Superstition is easy. You take it anyway. You hold it in your fist the whole way home.

choices.text: Pin it on your fridge
choices.consequence: You put it on the fridge where your mom and Gia will see it every morning, which makes it partly theirs, which is most of the point.

choices.text: Carry it in your pocket every day
choices.consequence: You keep it in your pocket and touch it at red lights, and by June the lettering on one side has worn completely smooth.

nodes.text: Fez tells you about the bakery in the walk-in cooler, quietly, like it's contraband. Small place on Marlow, ovens included in the lease, previous tenant gave up. He wants you managing it. Four a.m. starts, thirty hours minimum, actual paperwork with your actual name on it. He says all of it fast and then studies the floor. Nobody has ever offered you a future that came with a key.

choices.text: Accept the job
choices.consequence: You say yes standing in a cooler at thirty-six degrees, and Fez shakes your hand like a man who saw it done on television once.

choices.text: Negotiate fewer hours so you can keep writing
choices.consequence: You ask for four mornings instead of six, which costs you money, and he says fine immediately, and you learn that asking was allowed the whole time.

nodes.text: Six months and one health inspection later. There's a folding table by the register with a sheet cake on it that Fez bought instead of baking, which everybody finds funny except Fez. Your mom is there in her good coat. Gia photographs the sign from four angles. Marsha says four sentences and one of them is about her own first job at sixty days sober. Fez decides the oven needs him.

choices.text: Take a photo for the year
choices.consequence: You get everybody into one badly framed picture with half of Fez cut off at the edge, and it's on your mom's refrigerator inside a week.

choices.text: Just be there
choices.consequence: You put the phone face down on the counter and stand in the middle of it, and later you can't recall one detail except the noise of the room.

nodes.text: Not a book. Nine short essays, most of them bad, three of them not. You send one to a magazine that pays in contributor copies and they take it. Seeing your own sentences in a typeface you didn't choose does something specific to them: it puts the thing outside your body. The bakery is a job you happen to be good at. This is the first thing you'd call a project.

choices.text: Send the essay to Jules
choices.consequence: You send it to Jules with no message attached, which is either the bravest or the most cowardly available framing, and is probably both at once.

choices.text: Send it to your sponsor
choices.consequence: You send it to Ali, who reads slowly and takes two days about it, and you check your phone roughly four hundred times in those two days.

nodes.text: The email is long and arrives at three in the morning her time. She's proud of you and says it in a way that isn't a card. Then, halfway down, the rest: she isn't coming back to East Highland, not this year, probably not at all, and she'd like to keep writing to you. You read it four times looking for a door. There's no door. There's a window and it's open.

choices.text: Accept the letters as enough
choices.consequence: You write back the same night and ask her for nothing, and the not-asking is the most grown-up thing you have ever typed with your thumbs.

choices.text: Plan to visit her in a year, no pressure
choices.consequence: You put a date twelve months out in your phone with no expectations attached to it, and the date itself starts functioning as a kind of company.

nodes.text: He takes two days and sends back one line: you're writing the version of yourself the rest of us can actually read. You screenshot it, then print it, then buy a four-dollar frame at the drugstore. What you don't know, on this specific Thursday afternoon, is that his results came back Monday, and that he has decided to tell you in person, and that he's going to wait a month.

choices.text: Visit Ali in person next weekend
choices.consequence: You drive out Saturday for no stated reason and he makes you terrible tea, and you get a whole ordinary afternoon before you find out why it mattered.

choices.text: Send him a long thank-you letter
choices.consequence: You write four pages and mail them, and much later you find them in his kitchen drawer, folded, underneath the takeout menus he never threw away.

nodes.text: Five years. You hand your chip to a seventeen-year-old with bitten nails who came because a judge said so and stayed because of a doughnut. You're the one saying glad you're here now, in the same flat way, so it costs her nothing to receive it. You keep waiting to feel like you've arrived somewhere. You haven't. There's no door at the end of this. That's the good news.

choices.text: Stay in East Highland
choices.consequence: You sign a lease eight blocks from the bakery and stop describing this town, out loud or otherwise, as a place you are on your way out of.

choices.text: Move; keep the meetings the same
choices.consequence: You move an hour north and find a Tuesday room with identical bad coffee, and the sameness of it turns out to be the entire point.

nodes.text: Gia graduates in a gym that smells like floor polish and folding chairs. At dinner you stand up and say plain things: she did the reading, she made the food, she was thirteen. Your mom cries into a napkin and waves at you to keep going. Gia hugs you longer than her friends would find acceptable. You go to bed at ten, sober, full, tired in the way that's earned.

choices.text: Keep building the small life
choices.consequence: You go back to work on Monday, and somewhere in the second year the smallness of the life stops registering as a consolation prize.

choices.text: Travel for the first time in your life
choices.consequence: You buy a ticket to a city you have only ever seen on a screen, and the airport terrifies you, and you get on the plane.

nodes.text: Ali's chair was third from the left, near the radiator, because of his back. Nobody has sat in it since March. Tonight you get there early and sit down in it, and it's a chair, just a chair, and the room fills up the way rooms do. Somebody makes the coffee wrong. Somebody's phone goes off during the readings. You have a year ahead of you with a decision inside it.

choices.text: Hold the chair in East Highland
choices.consequence: You keep the Tuesday room and the key to the basement door, and being the person who unlocks it at seven turns out to be most of the job.

choices.text: Take meetings on the road
choices.consequence: You start going wherever the schedule takes you, and every basement in the country smells the same, which stops being funny and becomes a comfort.

nodes.text: You stay. East Highland does not transform; it gets marginally kinder, one block at a time, mostly because people you know are standing on those blocks. Over a decade you sponsor four people. Two get years. One relapses at eighteen months and comes back and is furious about it and stays. One you stop hearing from, and you keep his number in your phone anyway. Somewhere in there you learn the count was never the measure. The room is the measure. Chairs, urn, bad coffee, door unlocked at seven.

You go. Portland, Tucson, a church hall in Glasgow with an actual kettle and a plate of biscuits. The meetings are startlingly identical everywhere: same three opening sentences, same folding chairs, somebody's kid asleep under a coat in the back. You write in the mornings from cafés in cities you used to look up at fourteen and assume you would not live long enough to see. It turns out recovery packs completely flat and travels anywhere at all. It turns out, after everything, so do you.
